sections.name: The Self
sections.line: Everything here turns on one centre. Jung calls it the self: not the ego but the whole psyche, conscious and unconscious together, known only through its symbols.

quotes.text: Psychologically the self is a union of conscious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine). It stands for the psychic totality.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: Empirically, however, the self appears spontaneously in the shape of specific symbols, and its totality is discernible above all in the mandala and its countless variants.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

sections.name: Energy
sections.line: Jung's break with Freud began over one word. Libido stops meaning sexual desire and becomes psychic energy as such: a quantity that can flow into anything.

quotes.text: We would be better advised, therefore, when speaking of libido, to understand it as an energy-value which is able to communicate itself to any field of activity whatsoever, be it power, hunger, hatred, sexuality, or religion, without ever being itself a specific instinct.

All psychological phenomena can be considered as manifestations of energy, in the same way that all physical phenomena have been understood as energic manifestations ever since Robert Mayer discovered the law of the conservation of energy.

sections.name: Compensation
sections.line: The unconscious does not only hold what we push away. It answers the conscious attitude by supplying what that attitude leaves out, which is why Jung read most dreams as compensations.

quotes.text: Whereas Adler restricts his concept of compensation to the balancing of inferiority feelings, I conceive it as functional adjustment in general, an inherent self-regulation of the psychic apparatus.
That would not be impossible, for in my experience the vast majority of dreams are compensatory.
They always stress the other side in order to maintain the psychic equilibrium.

sections.name: Enantiodromia
sections.line: Push a one-sided attitude far enough and its opposite rises from the unconscious. Jung took the word from Heraclitus and used it for one life and for whole ages.

quotes.text: I use the term enantiodromia for the emergence of the unconscious opposite in the course of time.

In accordance with the principle of compensation which runs through the whole of nature,, every psychic development, whether individual or collective, possesses an optimum which, when exceeded, produces an enantiodromia, that is, turns into its opposite.
Then comes the enantiodromia: the steady forward movement no longer denotes an increase, but a decrease, in strength.

sections.name: The transcendent function
sections.line: When conscious and unconscious are held together, rather than one defeating the other, something appears that neither side contained. Jung called that process the transcendent function.

quotes.text: This function of mediation between the opposites I have termed the transcendent function, by which I mean nothing mysterious, but merely a combined function of conscious and unconscious elements, or, as in mathematics, a common function of real and imaginary quantities.
The psychological "transcendent function" arises from the union of conscious and unconscious contents.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.name: Functions
sections.line: Jung on the four functions and the two attitudes in Psychological Types (CW6, 1921: the introduction and the definitions) and in the papers of 1923, 1931 and 1936 appended to it; with CW11 ¶246 and the Zarathustra seminar on four aspects of orientation.

quotes.text: I distinguish four basic functions in all, two rational and two irrational (qq.v.): thinking and feeling, sensation and intuition (qq.v.).

Sensation and intuition I call irrational functions, because they are both concerned simply with what happens and with actual or potential realities. Thinking and feeling, being discriminative functions, are rational.

Sensation establishes what is actually present, thinking enables us to recognize its meaning, feeling tells us its value, and intuition points to possibilities as to whence it came and whither it is going in a given situation.
The four functions are somewhat like the four points of the compass; they are just as arbitrary and just as indispensable.
The four functions therefore form, when arranged diagrammatically, a cross with a rational axis at right angles to an irrational axis.
So, too, there are four aspects of psychological orientation, beyond which nothing fundamental remains to be said.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: Recapitulating, I would like to stress that each of the two general attitudes, introversion and extraversion, manifests itself in a special way in an individual through the predominance of one of the four basic functions.

These contrary attitudes are in themselves no more than correlative mechanisms: a diastolic going out and seizing of the object, and a systolic concentration and detachment of energy from the object seized.
Then if you follow it up psychologically, you arrive at the fact that consciousness has four corners as it were, four different ways or aspects, which we call the four functions.

cite.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

quotes.text: Very frequently, indeed as a general rule, a man identifies more or less completely with the most favoured and hence the most developed function.

number.line: Jung writes that numbers were as much found as invented and have a relative autonomy like that of the archetypes (CW8 ¶871). The QL framework names six positions, #0 to #5, and the site sets the numbers one to six beside them, as the owner has ruled. Each position shows the framework's words, von Franz on the number, and passages of Jung chosen for it.

jung.text: From this it follows irrefutably that the unconscious uses number as an ordering factor.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: I must confess that I incline to the view that numbers were as much found as invented, and that in consequence they possess a relative autonomy analogous to that of the archetypes.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: Accordingly it would seem that natural numbers have an archetypal character.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

series.text: Numbers then become typical psychophysical patterns of motion about which we can make the following statements: One comprises wholeness, two divides, repeats, and engenders symmetries, three centers the symmetries and initiates linear succession, four acts as a stabilizer by turning back to the one as well as bringing forth observables by creating boundaries, and so on.

pauli.text: Pauli concluded that natural numbers are the most primitive archetypes—inside and outside at once, devised by mind and discovered as order.

ql.name: The Origin / 0
ql.text: The indeterminate ground before anything is spoken. Pure capacity.

numbers.line: The framework's #0 beside the number one. Von Franz writes that quantitatively the one forms the unit and qualitatively contains the whole sequence of natural numbers; the Jung passage says the psychic structure is something given, the precondition found to be present in every case.

quotes.text: It thus possesses the following complementary dual aspect: quantitatively it forms the unit, qualitatively it contains the whole sequence of natural numbers.
Its “unit” character arises through a kind of kenösis (2 Cor. 8: 9) out of the All-Unity, and in this manner the one becomes the principium individuationis.

jung.text: The structure is something given, the precondition that is found to be present in every case.

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

ql.name: State 00
ql.text: The indeterminate relating to the indeterminate. Pure potentiality, the psychoid shadow where forms remain asleep.

numbers.line: The framework's #1 beside the number two. Von Franz writes that twoness signifies oscillation and rhythm but not yet linear time; Jung places the archetype as such at the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum and says it does not appear, in itself, to be capable of reaching consciousness.

quotes.text: In this context, twoness signifies oscillation and rhythm, but not yet linear time.

The dualism of zero and one, or one and two, furthermore, contains within itself the potential concept of fourfoldness (0--1--1--2). as well as that of three (0-1-2), if one is taken to be the mid-axis between zero and two.

jung.text: The archetype as such is a psychoid factor that belongs, as it were, to the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: It does not appear, in itself, to be capable of reaching consciousness.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

ql.name: State 01
ql.text: The indeterminate relating to the determinate. The emergence of form, the intrusion of the archetype into lived experience.

numbers.line: The framework's #2 beside the number three. Von Franz writes that three represents the unitary aspect of the bipolar one-continuum that has become conscious, and that three is often connected with time; Jung writes that archetypes have a numinous character, which can be healing or destructive but never indifferent.

quotes.text: According to this view the three then represents the unitary aspect of the bipolar one-continuum that has become conscious.
This is the reason why in number symbolism three is so often connected with time.

jung.text: That is, the archetypes have, when they appear, a distinctly numinous character which can only be described as "spiritual," if "magical" is too strong a word.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: It can be healing or destructive, but never indifferent, provided of course that it has attained a certain degree of clarity.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

ql.name: State 10
ql.text: The determinate relating to the indeterminate. The ego reaching back toward the unconscious, the act of symbol-making.

numbers.line: The framework's #3 beside the number four. Von Franz writes that attempts to establish an orientation toward wholeness possess a quaternary structure; Jung writes that images of wholeness are as a rule quaternities (CW8 ¶870), that the tendencies of conscious and unconscious together make up the transcendent function, and what he means by a symbolic expression.

quotes.text: The fact that mankind's repeated attempts to establish an orientation toward wholeness possess a quaternary structure appears to correspond to an archetypal psychic structural predisposition in man.
They are as a rule quaternities (or their multiples).

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: The tendencies of the conscious and the unconscious are the two factors that together make up the transcendent function.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

jung.text: A view which interprets the symbolic expression as the best possible formulation of a relatively unknown thing, which for that reason cannot be more clearly or characteristically represented, is symbolic.

ql.name: State 11
ql.text: The determinate relating to the determinate. Conscious rationality, the explicit mapping of known terms.

numbers.line: The framework's #4 beside the number five. Von Franz writes that the step to five is described in medieval natural philosophy as the quinta essentia included in the concept of the philosophers' stone; Jung writes that directed thinking imitates the succession of objectively real things in the same causal sequence, and that the ego is the complex factor to which all conscious contents are related.

quotes.text: It is included in the concept of the “philosophers’ stone” as the quinta essentia.

jung.text: To that extent, directed or logical thinking is reality-thinking, a thinking that is adapted to reality, by means of which we imitate the successiveness of objectively real things, so that the images inside our mind follow one another in the same strictly causal sequence as the events taking place outside it.
We understand the ego as the complex factor to which all conscious contents are related.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

ql.name: The Synthesis / 1
ql.text: The final return where the structure recognises itself. The quintessence that gathers the fourfold back into unity.

numbers.line: The framework's #5 beside the number six. Von Franz writes that six is the first numeral of the series to represent the sum of its divisors; Jung writes that the self is not only the centre but also the whole circumference which embraces conscious and unconscious.

quotes.text: For instance, it 15 immediately evident to us that six is the first numeral of the series to represent the sum of its divisors (one, two, and three).

jung.text: The self is not only the centre, but also the whole circumference which embraces both conscious and unconscious; it is the centre of this totality, just as the ego is the centre of consciousness.

psychoid.line: Jung writes that on account of its irrepresentable nature he has called the archetype psychoid (CW8 ¶840); von Franz writes that Jung expressly stated that his archetypes possess a psychoid aspect overlapping outer material reality.

quotes.text: It cannot be directly perceived or "represented," in contrast to the perceptible psychic phenomena, and on account of its "irrepresentable" nature I have called it "psychoid."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: He thus overlooks the fact that Jung expressly stated that his archetypes possess a “psychoid” aspect overlapping outer material reality.

ql.text: The archetype, as Jung finally understood it, is psychoid: it is as much inside as outside, an ordering pattern that manifests simultaneously in the soul's images and the world's matter.

time.line: Von Franz writes that linear or cyclical time does not initially exist; in the seminar on children's dreams Jung names the lion-headed Aion as the god of time who combines the opposites; and in CW8 ¶963 Jung and Pauli set synchronicity, an inconstant connection through meaning, beside causality in a quaternio with indestructible energy and the space-time continuum.

quotes.text: In other words, linear or cyclical time does not initially exist.
This is the deus leontocephalus, that is, Aion, meaning infinitely long time, the god of time who combines the opposites.

cite.workTitle: Children's Dreams: Notes from the Seminar 1936-1940

quotes.text: The image of wholeness then remains in the unconscious, so that on the one hand it shares the archaic nature of the unconscious and on the other finds itself in the psychically relative space-time continuum that is characteristic of the unconscious as such.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

intro.text: We finally agreed on the following quaternio:

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

terms: Inconstant Connection through Contingence, Equivalence, or "Meaning" (Synchronicity)

vaneenwyk.line: Van Eenwyk on the synchronic and the diachronic dynamics of the psyche; both quotations are his own words.

quotes.text: Fully aware of this, Jung developed the idea that the diachronic dynamics of development unfold from the synchronic dynamics.
Then, the relatively automatic processes of synchronic dynamics can generate diachronic dynamics, which are the developmental processes of the individual.
